en: The Sutra on the Swift Path of Transcending Saṃsāra through Mindfulness of the Buddha begins with the recitation of the Buddha’s praise:
The body of Amitābha Buddha is golden in color; His marks and signs and radiant light are peerless.
The white curl of hair winds like five Mount Sumerus; The deep blue eyes are as clear as the four great oceans.
Within his light, countless billions of transformation Buddhas appear, And the hosts of transformed Bodhisattvas are likewise boundless.
With forty-eight vows to deliver sentient beings, He causes those of all nine grades to ascend to the other shore.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha (recite one hundred times, one thousand times, or even ten thousand times; the more, the better, according to one's aspiration).
Homage to Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (ten times). Homage to Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta (ten times).
Homage to the Bodhisattvas of the Pure Great Ocean Assembly (ten recitations).
Having completed the recitation, recite the Verse for Dedication and Aspiration:
The Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, Amitābha is foremost among them; Through the nine grades, they deliver all sentient beings.
Your majestic virtue is infinite; I now take great refuge in you. I repent for the sins of my three karmas.
Whatever merits and virtues I possess, I wholeheartedly dedicate them. May the response appear at will for those who recite the Buddha’s name together with me;
At the moment of death, the realm of the Western Land shall be clearly manifest before my eyes.
May all who see or hear [this] be diligent, And together be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. May they behold the Buddha and comprehend birth and death;
As the Buddha, may they deliver all beings. May boundless afflictions be severed, And immeasurable Dharma-gates be cultivated.
Vowing to deliver all sentient beings, May they all together attain the Way of Buddhahood.
Though space may come to an end, my vows shall be inexhaustible; May sentient and insentient beings alike attain the same wisdom of all conditions,
And may all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time [be honored].
Homage to all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha (three times). Having finished this recitation, join the palms, prostrate with the head, and withdraw.
This is the essential method for returning to the source; it is the divine prescription for liberation from suffering. To fail to encounter this gateway is truly to be lamented.

If you are unable to immediately renounce worldly attachments to practice with single-minded devotion, simply direct your mind toward the West each day and fix your mindfulness upon Amitābha Buddha, making a constant practice of reciting his name either a hundred or a thousand times. This method of *nienfo* leads directly to the pond of Ultimate Bliss.
Within [the lotus], the flower itself serves as the designation. As soon as diligence and indolence are distinguished, flourishing and withering differ abruptly.

At the time of death, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara holds this flower in his hand to welcome those who have practiced mindfulness of the Buddha; they sit within the flower and are reborn in that land.
When the flower opens, they behold the Buddha, and their joy is inexhaustible. If I were to deceive you, may I fall into the realm where tongues are plucked out.
In hell, those who have taken your place in reciting the Buddha’s name undergo great suffering. I urge you to develop faith and quickly cultivate the practices for the Pure Land;
do not wait until one day your skin is changed [by death], for even if there were a thousand Buddhas, they could hardly save you. Make haste to advance;
time does not wait for man. Reflect on this, reflect on this!
Originally established for those who are extremely busy, this morning practice is set as a regular routine that must not be interrupted for even a single day.

Beyond these regular practices, whenever there is leisure time, one should continue to treat the recitation of the Buddha’s name as a vital daily task—just like dressing or eating—never being able to be separated from it for even half a moment. This...
This accords precisely with what the ancients said: "In the morning it is Amitābha; in the evening it is Amitābha.

Even if one is as busy as an arrow, one does not depart from Amitābha. Each time you recite, there is no need to fixate on a specific number of repetitions, nor must you restrict yourself to the four-character or six-character phrases.
Whether reciting aloud or silently, simply maintain a sincere mind whenever you practice nianfo.
I take refuge. Let there not be even a hair’s breadth of external thoughts intermingled; only then is it true mindfulness. The *Tripitaka* states:
"A single recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.

If this were not true mindfulness, pure and earnest, how could such a great efficacy be possible? Recently, there has been a certain type of person who practices nianfo [reciting the Buddha's name]... [text truncated]

One may understand how to properly nurture the spirit of joy, yet one frequently gives rise to anger; furthermore, out of greed for food and drink, one slaughters living beings at will, claiming that this poses no obstacle to the practice of *nianfo*.
How could such a person realize that the two karmas of harboring resentment and harming life are the very things that most readily summon demonic obstacles?
When the time of death arrives and the realms of karma manifest before one, these deeds will entangle and obstruct, resulting in nothing but agony.
Suffering is a state of delirium; even the desire to recite the name of a single Buddha cannot be realized, let alone ten recitations.
Therefore, those who cultivate the Pure Land practice must understand that what they do now is the cause, and what they obtain at the moment of death is the fruit.
Seize this opportunity to joyfully refrain from killing; do not wait until the final moment to feel regret. Furthermore, there is another type of person who recites the Buddha’s name...
Those who claim that they have never committed any evil throughout their lives may not necessarily be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
however, they will surely attain peace and security in this life and prosperity in the next, which is sufficient to fulfill their wishes.
This is because their faith is not firm, and the Buddha cannot save them. One must know that in the past there was a butcher who had committed the ten evils and the five heinous crimes.

When the end of life arrives, one undergoes ten thousand forms of suffering and seeks only the moment of swift death. It is only at such a desperate time that one hears of this Dharma-door of the Ten Recitations.
In the midst of such urgency, one takes incense, places it in the palm of the hand, and burns it, striving for transcendence;
yet even so, one may still behold the Buddha’s welcoming guidance and attain rebirth in the lowest of the lower grades. How much more so for those who practice throughout their entire lives!
Since one has not even committed the ten evil deeds or the five heinous crimes, and moreover has developed faith early on, how could there be any reason for not attaining rebirth in the Pure Land?
Therefore, one should not seek the karmic rewards of future lives through the practice of nianfo;
for when those rewards are exhausted, one will inevitably suffer affliction once again. How can that possibly compare to transcending the cycle of saṃsāra? It is truly sufficient.
To eternally enjoy the supreme bliss of Sukhāvatī is excellent; however, one should simply seek that one’s parents attain rebirth there.
Whether for their protection from illness while alive, or for their posthumous dedication when they have passed away, these are all expressions of filial piety and can indeed be achieved.

Yet, for those whose parents are still living, it is better to exhort them to practice mindfulness themselves. As the former Chan Master Yì of Changlu exhorted Emperor Xiaowen: "If you can exhort your father..."
For a mother to cultivate the Pure Land is the height of filial piety. That people of the present age have been able to encounter this book is due to their karmic affinity;
they should therefore give rise to firm faith and exhort their parents, relatives, and friends to recite the Buddha’s name together. Do not let such an opportunity pass you by face-to-face.
Even if you are unable to persuade others to believe, at least you have come to understand that within heaven and earth, this [Pure Land] has always existed.
This is the Dharma-door for transcending saṃsāra and taking rebirth in Sukhāvatī. By listening to it repeatedly with the faculty of hearing, one will naturally develop faith over time.
As for abstaining from killing, one should merely consume the three kinds of pure meat and refrain from harming living beings;

this refers to the Buddhist principle of not seeing the slaughter with one's eyes, not hearing of the slaughter with one's ears, and not suspecting in one's mind that the animal was killed for one's sake.
This is called "the three kinds of pure meat," and it may be eaten. However, it is even better if one can maintain a vegetarian diet for many years.
In general, when cultivating pure karma, apart from reciting the Buddha’s name, one should solely chant the Pure Land mantra to deliver all sentient beings and ensure rebirth in the Western Paradise.
Anything else is unrelated to the Pure Land. Formerly, when Master Lianchi was approaching his death, [he said:]
Indeed, he saw the Buddha coming to welcome him. He then earnestly exhorted the assembly, saying: "Sincerely recite the Buddha’s name; do not change the subject.

One may see that the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, as well as the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, are all not equal to the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name as being foremost."
